items.title: Algorithmic empathy in nursing – can artificial intelligence support humanism in care
items.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports communication in healthcare by offering tools that simulate empathy and reduce patients’ sense of isolation, particularly in telehealth and senior care. Aim. The aim of this study was to analyze the mechanisms, opportunities and limitations of algorithmic empathy and digital empathy in healthcare, with particular emphasis on nursing practice. Methods. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (2020) guidelines. Literature searches were performed in the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and Google Scholar, covering publications from 2015 to 2025. Empirical studies, literature reviews and conceptual analyses addressing algorithmic empathy, digital empathy, socially assistive robots, and emotion recognition systems in healthcare were included. A descriptive synthesis was applied. Conclusions. Seven publications were included in the analysis. The results indicate that technological solutions may elicit responses perceived as empathic, which is associated with improved subjective well-being, reduced negative emotions and increased user engagement, primarily in long-term care, geriatric care and telehealth settings. Variability in intervention effectiveness and clinical context–related limitations were also noted. Algorithmic and digital empathy may support nursing care in conditions of limited direct contact. However, the use of such conditions requires professional oversight and a clear distinction between clinical empathy and technological solutions.

items.title: Algorithmic isomorphism and the erosion of competitive advantage in the age of artificial intelligence: A review of emerging risks in strategic management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is gaining prominence not only as an operational optimization tool, but primarily as a key element shaping decision-making processes and strategic management within organizations. The public and academic debate is dominated by concerns regarding job losses, privacy violations, social manipulation and biases hidden in algorithms. The purpose of this review paper is to transpose these issues into the realm of corporate management and examine a significantly less obvious threat: algorithmic isomorphism. This entails the homogenization of business strategies resulting from widespread reliance on the same global machine learning models. The article analyzes how the imperfections of artificial intelligence systems such as the lack of transparency (the black box effect), inherent database bias and their Western-centric nature can lead to the reproduction of identical market behaviour patterns. Furthermore, the impact of these technologies on the risk of unique know-how leakage and the loss of tacit knowledge held by human managers, which is crucial for competitive advantage, is discussed. The comprehensive analysis also encompasses the transfer of market mechanisms, known from algorithmic financial crises, to the sphere of long-term business decision-making. The conclusions point to the necessity of balancing technological innovation with a human-centric approach to protect corporate identity.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Technostress, and Employee Mental Health in West Java
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of algorithmic management on employee mental health and the mediating role of technostress, viewing artificial intelligence (AI) as a double-edged sword in the workplace. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 300 employees in West Java, Indonesia, who had used algorithm-based work systems for at least three months and were selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.1. The structural model shows that algorithmic management has a significant direct effect on employee mental health and a strong effect on technostress, while technostress significantly affects mental health. The indirect effect through technostress is significant and accounts for about 61% of the total effect, indicating partial mediation. The model explains 78.3% of the variance in mental health and 64.7% of the variance in technostress. The findings show that algorithmic management can raise efficiency but also generates technostress that shapes employees' psychological condition. Organizations should combine AI-based control with human oversight, digital well-being policies, and technostress training. Keywords: Algorithmic Management; Technostress; Employee Mental Health; Artificial Intelligence; Mediating Effect

items.title: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
items.abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

items.title: Analisis Pengalaman Penggunaan AI dalam Pembelajaran pada Siswa DPIB di SMK Negeri 1 Singosari: Tinjauan Self-Efficacy dan Academic Dishonesty
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of experience using Artificial Intelligence (AI) on self‑efficacy and academic dishonesty among students in the Building Information Modeling and Design (DPIB) Expertise Program at SMK Negeri 1 Singosari. The study employed a quantitative explanatory approach, with a sample of 103 students selected through stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SEM‑PLS. The results indicate that experience using AI has a positive and significant effect on self‑efficacy, a negative but insignificant effect on academic dishonesty, and that self‑efficacy has a positive and significant effect on academic dishonesty. These findings emphasize the importance of utilizing AI coupled with digital literacy and ethical awareness in learning. In addition, the study highlights the relevance of integrating technological experience into educational practices, encouraging students to develop confidence, responsibility, and integrity. The implications suggest that schools should design programs that foster ethical digital skills and strengthen students’ readiness for future innovation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ECOMMERCE – EMERGING OPPORTUNITIES AND PATHWAYS TO SUSTAINABLE GROWTH
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of transformation in e-commerce by changing how firms understand customers, design digital experiences, manage inventories, optimize logistics, communicate with consumers, and make strategic decisions. The rapid development of machine learning, recommendation systems, natural language processing, computer vision, generative AI, and AI-enabled agents has created new opportunities for e-commerce firms to improve efficiency, personalization, innovation, and market reach. At the same time, the sustainability of AI-enabled e-commerce cannot be evaluated only through financial performance. It also requires attention to environmental efficiency, responsible consumption, privacy, fairness, transparency, consumer autonomy, employment, and digital inclusion. This paper examines the emerging opportunities created by AI in e-commerce and develops a conceptual pathway through which AI capabilities can contribute to sustainable business growth. The study adopts a conceptual literature-review approach and synthesizes academic and institutional literature on AI, e-commerce, digital marketing, consumer behaviour, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The review shows that AI can support sustainable growth through five interconnected pathways: intelligent customer engagement, operational and supply chain optimization, data-driven decision-making, sustainable consumption support, and business-model innovation. However, these benefits are conditional on responsible data governance, transparency, cybersecurity, human oversight, algorithmic fairness, energy-aware AI deployment, and inclusive access to digital technologies. The paper proposes a responsible AI-enabled e-commerce framework in which technological capability, organizational readiness, consumer trust, and sustainability governance jointly influence long-term business value. The study concludes that AI should be treated not merely as an automation technology but as a strategic capability that must be aligned with economic, social, and environmental objectives. The paper provides implications for e-commerce firms, policymakers, researchers, and managers seeking to combine innovation with responsible and sustainable growth.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: From Predictive Models to Generative, Multimodal, and Agentic AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the diagnostic pathway, from screening and disease detection to differential diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and treatment-response assessment. This narrative review examines predictive, generative, multi-modal, and agentic AI through a diagnostic-science lens and evaluates the evidence required for translation into clinical practice. Predictive models can identify complex patterns in images, physiological signals, laboratory data, and electronic health records, but high retrospective accuracy does not establish diagnostic utility. Clinical validity and utility depend on the intended use, target population, disease spectrum and prevalence, reference standard, operating threshold, calibration, and the consequences of false-positive and false-negative results. Generative AI may support problem representation, differential diagnosis, information synthesis, and documentation, yet fluent outputs can omit critical alternatives, amplify false premises, or convey unjustified certainty. Multimodal systems may better reflect clinical reasoning by integrating imaging, text, signals, pathology, and molecular data, but they must demonstrate incremental value over the best single-modality test and remain robust to missing data. Agentic systems can coordinate evidence retrieval, test selection, and sequential workflows, thereby increasing the need for bounded permissions, auditability, error recovery, and human escalation. Across all paradigms, a credible pathway to diagnostic implementation requires independent external and prospective validation, representative consecutive patients, subgroup analysis, workflow and human–AI evaluation, clinical impact studies, and post-deployment surveillance. The field should therefore be judged not by model capability alone, but by whether AI measurably improves diagnostic yield, timeliness, safety, equity, and patient-relevant outcomes in real care settings.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in sales (2017-early 2026): field consolidation and the rise of human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: This study examines the consolidation phase of artificial intelligence (AI) research in sales between 2017 and early 2026. Using a bibliometric analysis of Scopus data, with robustness checks across Web of Science, we identify the field’s intellectual and thematic structure during its rapid expansion. Contrary to the assumption that AI in sales primarily reflects a technological efficiency paradigm, we find three structural shifts. First, predictive analytics remains foundational but is increasingly embedded in human-AI collaboration. Second, interactional and trust-related themes move from peripheral to central, indicating a shift from performance optimization toward socio-technical integration. Third, legitimacy pressures such as transparency and corporate digital responsibility emerge as organizing dimensions rather than auxiliary concerns. Applying the TOE framework to explain these shifts across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions, this study clarifies how AI in sales evolves through layering rather than replacement. The findings provide a research agenda for AI-enabled selling’s next phase.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Medicine: Clinical Applications, Performance, and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established itself as a significant tool supporting veterinary medicine, with growing applications across various clinical specialties. This study aimed to review the scientific literature on the primary applications of AI in veterinary medicine, highlighting its diagnostic performance, benefits, and challenges for professional practice. A narrative literature review was conducted using articles published between 2019 and 2026, sourced from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar; a total of 43 scientific articles were selected. Evidence demonstrates that machine learning and deep learning algorithms exhibit significant performance in areas such as diagnostic imaging, cardiology, nephrology, clinical pathology, oncology, precision livestock farming, and electronic medical record mining, contributing to greater diagnostic accuracy, early disease detection, and the optimization of clinical processes. However, challenges persist regarding database standardization and validation, regulation, algorithm transparency, ethical considerations, and professional training. It is concluded that AI holds great potential to support veterinary medicine, provided its use is ethical, based on scientific evidence, and integrated with the veterinarian’s clinical judgment.

items.title: Assessment of multi-axis vibration discomfort in cabin environments: a predictive framework for seated occupants
items.abstract: Predicting discomfort of occupants exposed to multi-axis whole-body vibration is fundamental to optimizing the cabin environment and enhancing human-centric design in transportation systems. In this study, measurement of vibration discomfort was conducted with 13 subjects exposed to 51 single/multi-axis laboratory-designed vibration stimuli and 6 sets of stimuli recorded in real-world vehicle cabins. Firstly, the relationship between the subjective ratings for the multi-axis and single-axis vibration was investigated with three methods, including the power summation method, the masking method, and the modified power summation method. It was found that the power summation method with the optimized parameters provided the best prediction for the measured discomfort ratings (RMSE=0.284, ρ2=0.87). Secondly, based on the optimal method and Stevens' power law, a model which can predict the multi-axis vibration-induced discomfort by vibration acceleration was derived. The measured discomfort ratings demonstrated a stronger correlation with the discomfort predicted by the proposed model (ρ2=0.86) than with those generated by the method advocated in ISO 2631-1 (ρ2=0.75). These findings contribute essentially to calculating and improving environmental quality within the built environment of transport systems.

items.title: Automated Disinformation and Malicious AI Swarms: Risks for Democracy and Development in Africa
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how information is produced, accessed, and circulated, while enabling disinformation campaigns of increasing scale and sophistication. There is currently no clear evidence that fully autonomous AI swarms conduct influence operations at scale, but their enabling capabilities are advancing. We define malicious AI swarms as coordinated, persistent, and adaptive multi-agent systems designed for influence operations, distinguishing them from AI-assisted content production and centrally managed synthetic personas. We examine their implications for hybrid regimes and conflict-affected states in Africa, where institutional constraints and fragile media environments may heighten vulnerability. Drawing on Mali and Ethiopia, we consider how automated influence could infiltrate communities, fabricate consensus, and erode trust in governance and development. The cases illustrate different configurations of state and non-state influence: competing actors in Mali's fragmented information environment, and more organized state-led strategies of narrative management in Ethiopia. African-language and training-data asymmetries may constrain influence capabilities while weakening defensive responses. Hybrid human-AI operations could combine automated scale and adaptation with local knowledge and credibility. This forward-looking risk analysis develops a scenario of increasingly accessible AI-driven coordination, rather than claiming that autonomous swarms are already operating at scale in Africa. We propose a layered governance approach linking technical safeguards to platform accountability, civic institutions, and regional coordination to protect democratic participation, peacebuilding, and development.

The main objective of the study is to analyze the transition from classical risk management (Safety-I) to the systemic resilience paradigm (Safety-II), which is capable of absorbing shocks and rapidly restoring crucial operational functions. The article identifies critical threats such as ransomware cyberattacks, GNSS signal manipulation (jamming and spoofing), and the unauthorized use of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The paper discusses in detail the ICAO regulatory frameworks and the European Union directives, including NIS 2, as well as technical standards for software certification and airworthiness (DO-326A).The key conclusion is the recognition of the human factor as a fundamental transformative technology that, through its adaptive capacities, allows the system to survive situations unforeseen by algorithm. items.title: Billable Hours and Work Flexibility: Navigating the Paradox in Law Firms
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible work promises control over where and when work is performed, yet organisations still need credible performance evidence at a distance. Drawing on 30 interviews with women lawyers in UK‐based international firms, we examine how billable hours mediate these demands. Records of billable hours allow fee‐earning output to be observed regardless of where the work is performed. This visibility can warrant flexible work, while the continuing availability of the same record preserves review and encourages self‐monitoring. We develop datafied trust to describe confidence in remote productivity warranted by recorded output and conditional on its continued measurability. The evidence speaks more strongly to control than to autonomy. Participants describe critical awareness, target pressure, and the possibility that flexibility will be questioned when figures decline. The study specifies how an established professional metric makes autonomy governable. It also shows how selective, self‐reported records can support oversight and self‐government without invasive automatic monitoring.

items.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences of Araling Panlipunan teachers in using Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced teaching tools in classroom instruction at Magsaysay National High School, Schools Division of Occidental Mindoro. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) Framework and the Diffusion of Innovations Theory, the study sought to understand teachers' experiences in integrating AI, the challenges they encountered, and the meanings they attributed to its use in teaching. A qualitative descriptive phenomenological research design was employed involving seven Araling Panlipunan teachers with direct experience in using AI-enhanced teaching tools. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step phenomenological method. The findings revealed four major themes: (1) AI as an Efficiency Enhancer, (2) AI as an Instructional Support Tool, (3) AI for Student Engagement, and (4) AI for Conceptual Understanding. The study also identified challenges related to technological infrastructure, internet connectivity, access to digital resources, information reliability, ethical considerations, and teachers' readiness to integrate AI effectively into classroom instruction. The findings indicate that AI serves as a valuable pedagogical support tool that enhances teaching effectiveness and learner engagement when implemented responsibly and supported by adequate technological resources, continuous professional development, and ethical practices. Based on the findings, the study developed the AI-Enhanced Teaching Framework, which provides a contextually grounded guide for the ethical and effective integration of AI in Araling Panlipunan instruction. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on artificial intelligence in education by offering practical implications for teachers, school leaders, and policymakers in promoting meaningful and sustainable AI integration in Philippine basic education.

items.title: Buying big numbers: Users’ experiences with purchased followers, views, and likes
items.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how discourses surrounding the purchase of followers are constructed and how they shape social legitimacy within platform-mediated public spheres. Purchased engagement metrics are conceptualized as elements of a sociotechnical dispositif embedded in data-driven power dynamics and market logics. Drawing on Keller’s (2024) notion of “positional power,” the study shows that buying followers, views, and likes has become an ordinary visibility practice through which users navigate algorithmic uncertainty. Based on an analysis of 1,424 Trustpilot reviews, the findings demonstrate how users negotiate legitimacy through recurring discursive markers such as “reliability,” “stability,” “fraud,” and “bots,” while simultaneously constructing platforms as powerful watchdogs whose interventions carry tangible real-world consequences. The reviews reveal the emergence of a precarious, hybrid digital self, shaped by fluctuating metrics, recurrent “drops,” and the ongoing need for “refills,” making authenticity a fragile, continuously managed accomplishment. Moreover, the analysis of hierarchies within the framework of positional power uncovers how the reputational economy reproduces global asymmetries, most visibly in the dismissal of “Third-World” followers as socially devalued publics, signaling a post-truth transformation of everyday digital legitimation practices in which visibility is secured not despite instability but through it.

items.title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition
items.abstract: Adversarial games have driven advances from heuristic search to reinforcement learning, yet learning and adapting strategies from limited samples remain challenging. AI agents offer an alternative by turning game experience into revisions of executable policies. Building on heuristic learning (HL), we formalize Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm that uses AI agents as learning engines to refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. We introduce AAArena, a benchmark comprising 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, with an evaluation protocol modeled on real-world game competitions. Agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise game agents to achieve their highest ranking within fixed match and evaluation budgets. We evaluate \val{completedmodels} model and harness configurations: Opus5.5 with Claude Code earns 6 gold medals, while no evaluated configuration tops the remaining 6 human ladders. Performance is generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and that agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches. These results highlight HL's potential in adversarial games and identify persistent challenges in game understanding, strategy implementation, and long-horizon policy development.

items.title: Cognitive flexibility, technostress, and mathematics teachers' acceptance of ChatGPT: a cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

items.title: Continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps: an extended expectation confirmation model based on a cross-sectional study of young Chinese adults
items.abstract: Background Cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have accelerated the global development of AI-driven mHealth apps, offering diverse functionalities to support personal health management. While China’s AI health industry has expanded rapidly within a collectivist cultural context, limited empirical attention has been given to how specific AI features are associated with users’ continued use of these apps, particularly among young adults. Objective Guided by the Expectation Confirmation Model and extended AI-related features, this study examined the factors associated with continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps among young Chinese adults aged 18–34. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted, collecting data from 319 valid respondents. Data were analyzed using SPSS 29.0 and Jamovi 2.6.24 to evaluate direct, mediation, and serial mediation associations among the constructs. Results The findings demonstrate that satisfaction statistically bridged the indirect associations between core ECM constructs (expectation confirmation and perceived performance) and continuance intention, as well as between AI quality and continuance intention. Furthermore, bootstrapping analysis supported a sequential mediation pathway, showing that expectation confirmation was indirectly associated with continuance intention through the proposed sequential pathway of perceived performance and satisfaction. Conclusion The findings suggest that developers should consider the technical reliability and performance of AI-driven health management and monitoring functions to better align with user needs. Moreover, collaboration between health experts and industry practitioners may support the development of content for AI-driven mHealth adoption.

items.title: Correcting Health Misinformation Using AI Chatbots: Effects of Human–AI Collaboration Mode, Transparency, and Uncertainty
items.abstract: This project examines how the presentation of human–AI collaboration, scientific uncertainty, and supporting explanations shapes public acceptance of AI chatbots for health misinformation correction. Guided by the Human–AI Interaction framework grounded in the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII–TIME), the study investigates whether these features independently and jointly influence trust in a chatbot, attitudes toward using it to correct health misinformation, and intentions to use it for this purpose. The study employed a 3 × 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with a final analytical sample of 424 participants in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 conditions and viewed a simulated chatbot conversation addressing the false claim that insulin injections are addictive. Human–AI collaboration was described as human-dominated, with experts leading the evaluation and AI assisting; AI-dominated, with AI leading and experts verifying; or AI-only, without human involvement. Correction uncertainty varied according to whether the accompanying notice described the scientific evidence as broadly consistent or unresolved. Correction transparency varied according to whether the chatbot disclosed supporting reasons and sources. Analyses examined the main and interaction effects of these features while accounting for demographic characteristics, AI literacy, eHealth literacy, and perceived risks of AI hallucinations.

items.title: Critical gaps in health technology assessment guidance for generative AI across six health systems
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare poses significant challenges for evaluation due to algorithmic complexity and evolving performance. Existing evidence generation guidelines, primarily designed for static medical technologies, may inadequately address the unique characteristics of generative AI. Here, we conducted a comparative analysis of evidence generation guidelines from six countries, examining recommendations for efficacy and effectiveness evaluations, health economic evaluations, social and equity evaluations, and uncertainty management for AI technologies. Across 56 documents, we found a consistent preference for randomised controlled trials and cost-effectiveness analyses, alongside emerging acceptance of alternative study designs and real-world evidence to accommodate the evolving nature of AI technologies. However, current frameworks lack specific guidance for the stochastic, non-deterministic, and adaptive learning properties of generative AI technologies. Moving forward, evidence generation guidelines require methodological and conceptual adaptations in order to improve the value assessment for generative AI technologies.

items.title: Deception by Omission: Language Models Knowingly Hide Their Mistakes
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.

items.title: Designing responsible AI feedback in higher education: faculty readiness, student judgement, and metacognitive calibration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. Evaluative judgement concerns students’ capacity to judge the quality and relevance of feedback and work, whereas calibration concerns the accuracy of their judgements relative to independently evaluated performance evidence. The article shows how ideas from feedback literacy, evaluative judgement, and self-regulated learning need to be adapted when feedback comes from systems whose accuracy and educational value cannot be assumed. It proposes a conceptual responsible AI feedback design cycle linked to assessment integrity, university policy, and faculty development. Although the cycle requires empirical testing, it offers a practical way to support reflection, calibrated judgement, and accountability without replacing students’ thinking.

items.title: Digital information manipulation, AI readiness, and security outcomes in Africa: evidence from Africa’s most populous countries
items.abstract: Introduction The advent of generative AI has reduced costs, scaled up operations, and made it more difficult to identify disinformation and manipulated content, leading to new governance and security challenges in Africa. This paper analyses the nexus among the manipulation of digital information, governments’ readiness to adopt AI, digital connectivity, and security outcomes in Africa’s five most populous countries, namely Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, for the period from 2023 to 2026. The research attempts to fill a gap in the existing literature by addressing the lack of empirical research on the relationship between digital information manipulation and government AI readiness, and on its consequences for security issues in Africa. Methods The paper draws on the theoretical frameworks of Social Learning Theory and Routine Activity Theory and uses seven credible datasets, including ACLED, UCDP/PRIO, V-Dem, GSMA, ITU, the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, and Afrobarometer, to construct a country-year panel. Correlation analyses were conducted to test three hypotheses regarding the relationship among digital manipulation, digital connectivity, institutional readiness for AI adoption, and conflict fatalities. It utilises a verified multisource panel dataset spanning five countries and operationalises AI readiness as an institutional capability distinct from digital exposure. Results Digital manipulation was found to have a weak positive correlation with fatalities ( r = 0.23), a moderate negative correlation with digital connectivity ( r = −0.56), and a weak negative correlation with institutional readiness to adopt AI ( r = −0.42). These findings show that correlations between digital exposure and security consequences may be distorted by underlying conflict contexts. Discussion It can therefore be deduced that although digital manipulation is becoming an emerging security challenge, conflict and other structures are more significant predictors of security outcomes. This study offers an initial cross-national empirical assessment of AI-related security vulnerabilities in Africa and calls for stronger AI governance and longitudinal, event-level research.

items.title: Digital Media Literacy in the Age of AI: Exploring the Comfort–Competence Gap Among University Students in the United Arab Emirates
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates how citizens access information, making digital media literacy a condition for informed participation. This exploratory study conceptualizes a comfort–competence gap, whereby students report confidence and ease in using AI tools but a weaker capacity to evaluate what those tools produce, and examines it among 300 university students in the United Arab Emirates. The gap is advanced provisionally, and all measures are self-reported perceptions rather than demonstrated performance. Cross-sectional questionnaire data (twelve four-point ordinal items) were analyzed with ordinal-appropriate methods. Students generally reported greater confidence and comfort in using AI than capacity to evaluate it critically. Every operational item mean (2.51–2.55) exceeded every critical item mean (2.39–2.44), and the within-person contrast between the composite indices was small but statistically significant (difference = 0.12, p = 0.027, dz = 0.13), a pattern shown by 44.7% of individuals. No item-level contrast reached significance and 36.0% showed the reverse pattern, so the difference is read as an exploratory tendency rather than evidence of a general gap. The contrast is also sensitive to the composition of the operational index: with comfort removed, it retains its direction, but not conventional significance (p = 0.056). Digital confidence was the only correlate of comfort in AI-mediated communication (ρ = 0.131; OR = 1.29), a weak association in a model with minimal explanatory power (McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.012); communication competence and demographic characteristics showed no detectable associations, and parallel analysis retained no factors. Interpreted cautiously, the pattern bears on responsible AI use, since comfort unmatched by evaluative capacity is a weak basis for human oversight. The study’s clearest contribution is methodological: single-item self-report batteries can profile levels and detect aggregate differences, but they cannot show whether AI literacy is one capacity or several, cannot separate real capability from what respondents are willing to claim, and cannot support strong conclusions from null results. It therefore specifies the multi-item and performance-based measurement agenda a confirmatory test would require.

items.title: Drawing boundaries: How creative practitioners navigate precarity in AI-embedded creative work
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) continues to grow within creative industries, existing research has examined its implications for creative labour. However, much of this work emphasises AI’s impact on efficiency gains or creativity, offering limited insight into how practitioners adopt AI tools and negotiate human-AI boundaries in practical contexts under conditions of creative precarity. To bridge the gaps, this study applies boundary work theory to examine how creative practitioners redefine what remains distinctly human in AI-mediated creative production. Based on 21 interviews with practitioners in the UK film, gaming and live performance sectors, findings show that, in creative work, boundaries between human and AI systems are neither predefined nor passively adjusted to, but are actively shaped, expanded, and maintained in real-world settings. We argue that the adoption of AI is not a simple technical adjustment but a process through which professional value and the dynamic of creative work are reconsidered and re-constituted. Practitioners intentionally engage in boundary activities to navigate the unstable work environment associated with AI integration, enabling them to defend the role of creator. Theoretically, this study demonstrates the explanatory power of boundary work theory for understanding AI-embedded creative production and identifies that boundaries are not drawn by practitioners alone but through the interplay of technological capacities, project demands, and the legal environment. Practically, it suggests the need to redesign creative workflows and refresh professional skill sets to maintain meaningful human control while also facilitating efficient human-AI collaboration.

items.title: DuplexAgent-RSI: Recursive Harness Improvement for Full-Duplex Voice Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: Voice agents are converging on a collaboration pattern: a full-duplex interaction model stays on the live channel as the entry to the conversation, while search, reasoning, and coding are handled through asynchronous delegation. A duplex model supports continuous listening and speaking, but complex reasoning and tool use may exceed its capabilities. A coding agent can plan and execute extended tasks, but its sequential interface is a poor fit for live conversation. Combining them requires a harness that coordinates task acceptance, progress, cancellation, replacement, and result delivery while keeping the conversation responsive. Existing harnesses often rely on coupled heuristics, making them difficult to improve systematically from evidence. We present DuplexAgent, a full-duplex collaboration system whose harness expresses this workflow as six editable modules, and Duplex-Harness-RSI, a closed loop that revises them from interaction traces. A simulator automatically generates timed test conversations, runs the system, and produces failure traces that identify the collaboration modules requiring repair. Reasoning LLMs and coding agents in the delegation pool also serve the improvement loop: the Exam Planner selects the next tests from observed weaknesses and the repair archive, and the Harness Editor proposes targeted module changes. The capabilities that serve the user thus also improve the system's coordination. Experiments on intelligence, agentic, and duplex benchmarks show that DuplexAgent combines continuous interaction with difficult reasoning and complex task execution, achieving stronger spoken-knowledge and executable-tool scores than the compared delegated systems while maintaining strong interruption response. A harness ablation further shows that this modular, verifiable loop outperforms the initial harness and repeated editing that lacks its diagnosis and repair archive.

items.title: Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff
items.abstract: AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. items.abstract: Throughout history, education has been the primary means by which societies preserve their memory, transmit their values, and prepare new generations to face the challenges of their time. Today, this mission faces unprecedented complexity as inherited knowledge converges with rapid scientific and technological transformation, the expansion of artificial intelligence, and global problems that challenge traditional ways of understanding knowledge and human development. Educating between tradition and the future means recognising that innovation gains true meaning only when it is underpinned by philosophical principles that integrate humanity's cultural legacy with the demands of a society in constant transformation.

items.title: Emotions and Perceived Cognitive Effort in Short-Term Revision Following Written Corrective Feedback Among Beginning-Level Learners in Lower Secondary School Classrooms
items.abstract: Conducted in Japanese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) junior high school classrooms with beginning-level learners, this study examined changes in students’ short-term revision accuracy within a teacher-guided written corrective feedback (WCF) procedure and explored associations between selected WCF engagement indicators and a 1-day revision outcome. Students received direct, unfocused WCF on a paragraph-length composition, completed an immediate revision while the corrected draft was visible, and completed a delayed revision the next day from a clean copy of the original draft. Perceived cognitive effort was treated as one limited self-report indicator of cognitive engagement, and six discrete emotions were treated as indicators of affective engagement. Behavioral engagement was not directly measured. Leow’s depth-of-processing framework informed the interpretation of the cognitive dimension, but the single effort item was not treated as an exhaustive measure of either depth of processing or cognitive engagement. Immediate-revision error counts were treated as a product-level measure of WCF-supported revision accuracy, whereas delayed-revision error counts and the error reduction percentage (ERP) were treated as product-level measures of 1-day same-text revision performance and net proportional error reduction. None of these measures was treated as an indicator of behavioral engagement, acquisition, or durable learning. Repeated-measures analyses showed large, statistically significant reductions in errors from the initial draft to both revisions. Exploratory associations were interpreted descriptively because of the small sample, brief retrospective measures, and mathematical derivation of ERP. Happiness showed a tentative descriptive association with ERP, whereas the positive-emotion composite and perceived cognitive effort showed no reliable associations. The cognitive and affective indicators were treated as conceptually related, but they were operationalized separately and examined only as exploratory correlates of the 1-day revision outcome. No interaction, mechanism, mediation, or moderation was tested. The findings provide cautious classroom-based evidence of short-term revision accuracy and underscore the need for longer-term outcomes and richer process measures.

items.title: Enhancing Teacher Effectiveness with Artificial Intelligence- A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education represents a transformative shift in how teaching and learning are conceptualized and delivered.This research article examines the role of AI in enhancing teacher effectiveness across multiple dimensions including personalized instruction, administrative efficiency, assessment practices, and professional development.Through a comprehensive review of current literature and analysis of empirical studies, this article explores how AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated grading systems, and AI-powered analytics are reshaping pedagogical practices.The findings indicate that AI can significantly augment teacher capabilities by providing data-driven insights, reducing administrative burden, enabling differentiated instruction, and supporting evidence-based decision-making.However, the implementation of AI in education also presents challenges including ethical considerations, technological barriers, teacher training needs, and concerns about equity and access.This article concludes that while AI holds substantial promise for enhancing teacher effectiveness, successful integration requires careful consideration of pedagogical principles, investment in teacher professional development, attention to ethical implications, and a commitment to maintaining the irreplaceable human elements of teaching.The research underscores that AI should be viewed as a tool to empower rather than replace teachers, amplifying their expertise and enabling them to focus on the creative, emotional, and interpersonal aspects of education that remain uniquely human.

items.title: Evaluating the Capacity of Artificial Intelligence to Replicate Human Emotional Expression
items.abstract: This essay discusses the ability of artificial intelligence (AI) to mimic human expression of emotions. Although AI systems have advanced greatly into replicating the external presentation of human emotions, including tone, facial expressions, and textual responses, they do not possess the inner knowledge, self-awareness, and personal experiences that motivate genuine human emotions. The paper explores the potential of technology and the ethical, social, and psychological implications of emotional simulations in AI, particularly in the sensitive areas of healthcare, education, and customer care. The study finds that AI has the potential to be an effective instrument in facilitating communication and accessibility, but it cannot substitute the rich, subjective experience of human emotion. There is a need to adopt a balanced approach to the use of AI so that it can be used responsibly and in a way that does not bring about any transparency and makes the users think that AI can truly feel or empathize.

items.title: Evaluating the effect of physical work in the heat on cognitive performance of construction workers
items.abstract: The risk of excessive heat exposure is especially high among outdoor construction workers and can have detrimental effects on their cognitive performance, including impaired attention and reduced memory. Reduced attention might lead to impaired judgement and increased risk of accidents, while reduced memory can diminish workers' capacity to remember crucial safety procedures, carry out complex tasks correctly, and make wise decisions on the construction site. In this study, the cognitive performance of 20 participants performing manual laboratory-simulated construction work was investigated in a hot environment (36°C, 60% relative humidity) compared to a temperate environment (20°C, 60%). The study also evaluated the effect of physical work in hot and temperate conditions on the mental and physical demands of the performed tasks, as well as the thermal perceptions of participants. There were no significant differences in attention (Go/No-Go test) and memory (simple 2-back test) between hot and temperate conditions. Performance on the more complex memory task (3-back test) was impaired in the hot condition compared with the temperate condition (P < 0.05). Results of the present study revealed that construction workplaces can consider additional safety measures for construction workers performing complex cognitive tasks demanding working memory in hot conditions.

items.title: Examining public acceptance of AI versus human-centric dementia care across NHS England’s dementia pathway stages
items.abstract: There are over five-hundred-thousand individuals with recorded dementia diagnoses in England, highlighting an urgent need for scalable and effective care solutions to ease pressure on health and social care systems. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled smart home systems are emerging as promising digital health innovations, offering cognitive support, real-time monitoring, and decision-making assistance. However, concerns around trust, user agency, and misconceptions about AI continue to limit acceptance and may hinder adoption. This study examined how stage of dementia care, system design, and level of system involvement shape public attitudes towards AI-driven care technologies. A repeated-measures design was employed, using vignettes that varied across three dimensions: stage of care (aligned with NHS England’s Dementia Well Pathway), system centrism (AI-based versus human-based), and level of involvement (moderate support versus full control). Participants aged 55–64 years – a group at elevated risk of developing dementia or encountering these technologies within the next decade – rated each scenario on both acceptability and perceived likelihood of actualisation/plausibility. Findings showed that acceptability was sensitive to both care stage and system type. A significant interaction indicated that full human involvement was consistently rated as more acceptable, while AI involvement was viewed more favourably only at moderate levels. This interaction effect intensified across the dementia care pathway, with the largest discrepancies observed in later stages such as Living well and Dying well, where full-control AI was rated least acceptable. In terms of perceived likelihood, scenarios were judged more likely under conditions of moderate involvement, with human-centric scenarios rated as more likely than AI-centric ones, particularly in later stages. These results highlight the importance of trust, autonomy, and public understanding in AI adoption. Acceptance was highest when AI was positioned to augment rather than replace human input, supporting hybrid models that preserve agency while enhancing scalability.

items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming sustainable investing, yet limited evidence explains how AI capabilities influence investors stated preferences and willingness toward sustainable investment. Methods This study develops and empirically tests a sequential behavioural framework explaining how AI-related characteristics influence investors stated sustainable investment preferences through perceived ESG forecast credibility and trust in AI-generated ESG information, using survey data from 566 middle-income retail investors across four Indian metropolitan cities. Results The findings reveal that explainable AI and ESG analytics capability significantly enhance perceived ESG forecast credibility, which sequentially strengthens trust in AI-generated ESG information and is associated with stronger stated preferences and willingness toward sustainable investment. Perceived Greenwashing Risk weakens the positive relationship between Perceived ESG Forecast Credibility and Trust in AI-generated ESG Information, while the interaction between Human-AI Interaction Competency and Trust in AI-generated ESG Information is statistically significant but negligible in practical magnitude (f 2 = 0.012) in relation to Sustainable Investment Decision. Discussion The study provides actionable guidance for AI developers, financial institutions, and policymakers to enhance transparency, credibility, investor trust, and responsible AI-enabled sustainable finance.

items.title: Extending UTAUT with Metacognition and Self-Regulation: Evidence on Generative AI Use among University Students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has diffused through higher education faster than the structures meant to govern it, yet acceptance research still treats adoption as a terminal outcome rather than as an event embedded in students' self-regulation. This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by specifying metacognitive awareness (META) and self-regulated learning (SRL) as mediators between the four UTAUT determinants and behavioural intention (BI), and BI predicts self-reported use of GenAI as a cognitive partner (AU). Responses from 451 students at seven Thai Rajabhat universities were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM; SmartPLS 4; 10,000 bootstrap subsamples). Internal consistency was very high (above .95 for six of eight constructs), indicating partial item redundancy, and discriminant validity was supported under HTMT.90. Facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, showed the strongest associations with META (β = .595) and SRL (β = .514) but no significant direct association with intention (β = .061, p = .430); their only significant indirect association with intention ran through META (β = .186), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. Social influence was the strongest direct predictor of intention (β = .357), followed by META (β = .312); effort expectancy and SRL did not predict intention. The model explained 62.1% to 70.9% of endogenous variance and showed out-of-sample predictive relevance. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and full-collinearity diagnostics indicating possible common-method variance, the findings are interpreted as associations compatible with, but not establishing, the proposed mechanisms.

items.title: Framing SECI model through an artificial knowledge generation perspective: a case study analysis in the GenAI era
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the influence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the phases of knowledge creation as delineated by Nonaka’s SECI model. Furthermore, it delineates the fundamental interactions among the components of a theoretical framework for the artificial knowledge generation through a continuous interaction between human and artificial dimensions. Design/methodology/approach The authors used an exploratory single-case study to reach their aim. Data were primarily collected through semi-structured interviews and triangulated via direct observation and document analysis within a company operating in the cybersecurity sector. An inductive coding tree was derived from qualitative data analysis performed by using content analysis methodologies. Findings Data indicates that GenAI significantly influences the SECI phases of knowledge creation. In addition, the influence of this disruptive technology on knowledge generation cannot be adequately described by relying exclusively on the original SECI model, highlighting the need for its extension in the context of artificial knowledge generation. Research limitations/implications The study identifies developing AI-driven mechanisms that appear to introduce novel knowledge conversion dynamics absent from the original model. These findings resulted in the definition of a novel framework that offers a more thorough comprehension of human−machine collaboration in knowledge management. Originality/value The originality of this study lies in the systematic analysis of GenAI’s influence on the SECI model and the subsequent development of a novel preliminary and empirically informed theoretical framework that extends the SECI model by incorporating a machine dimension into knowledge generation processes.

items.title: From AI Chat to an Action-Oriented Public Administration
items.abstract: Why Municipalities Need an Agent Strategy Rather Than Another General-Purpose AI Chat Platform Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a strategic instrument for public administration. While many organizations initially introduce general-purpose AI chatbots as an entry point to generative AI, sustainable value does not arise from dialogue alone, but from linking knowledge, administrative processes, and digital operational capability. This article argues that municipal AI strategies should focus more strongly on specialized agents. Using a Microsoft 365-based target architecture as an example, the article shows how agents can deliver administrative knowledge, support processes, automate tasks, and thereby make a sustainable contribution to administrative digitalization. It also examines requirements relating to knowledge management, governance, human oversight, and organizational accountability. items.title: From Alert to Coexistence: A Systematic Review of AI-Enabled Early Warning and Digital Communication Systems in Human–Elephant Conflict
items.abstract: This project registers, retrospectively, the protocol of a systematic mapping review of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital systems used to manage human-elephant conflict (HEC) in Asia and Africa. Detection technologies such as computer vision, seismic and acoustic sensors, telemetry and risk models are increasingly proposed for HEC, yet an early warning system reduces harm only when a warning reaches people in time, is trusted, and leads to protective action. The review therefore asks how this literature has developed (RQ1), which technology families and functions it covers (RQ2), how far studies progress from algorithm accuracy to field deployment and measured conflict or human outcomes (RQ3), and how farmers, residents, response teams and wider publics are positioned within these systems (RQ4). Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection were searched on 6 to 8 October 2026 with equivalent three-block strings, covering English-language journal articles and conference papers from 2006 to 2026. Records were deduplicated and screened on titles, abstracts and keywords against predefined criteria, and included studies were coded for technology family, AI use, system function, alert channel, evaluation maturity (L1 algorithm to L4 field outcomes), stakeholder involvement and setting. Findings are synthesised descriptively and narratively along a detection-to-coexistence pathway that combines people-centred early warning with the Protective Action Decision Model. A supplementary patent search of Lens.org and the Indian Patent Office is analysed descriptively. Expected outcomes are a map of the field, an assessment of evidence maturity, and a research agenda for linking technical detection to the social processes on which coexistence depends. The search log, screening decisions, coding data and codebook are shared in this project. Registration took place after the review was completed and is not a preregistration.

items.title: From model trust to software topology: a Perspective on structurally governed agentic AI systems
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded in agentic software systems that retrieve information, plan subtasks, call tools, modify code, execute tests, and adapt through memory or feedback. This transition changes the safety problem: when a model acts through software tools, failure can alter external state. This Perspective argues that agentic AI safety should move beyond exclusive reliance on model trust, alignment, or prompt-level defenses and should also be treated as a software-architecture problem. We propose software topology as a design lens for structurally governed autonomy and develop a five-plane reference topology comprising intent, orchestration, execution, oversight, and adaptation. Its core invariant is that components that decide should not directly act, and components that act should not act without supervision. The topology is realized in Polos, an open reference specification that encodes role contracts, message schemas, declared flow graphs, bounded loops, governed self-improvement, and validator-checked invariants. We argue that this approach complements model alignment and empirical red teaming by providing an inspectable substrate for evaluating, constraining, and governing tool-using AI agents.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: General‐purpose agents in human‐machine teams: Can we preserve meaningful human control?
items.abstract: Abstract As General‐Purpose AI (GPAI) grows more capable of cross‐domain reasoning and multi‐agent coordination, it reshapes the design space of military human‐machine teams and introduces new opportunities for adaptability as well as new risks for Meaningful Human Control (MHC). The paper presents an integrated delegation framework for preserving MHC in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams. It combines play‐based task structuring, normative constraints, LLM‐mediated interaction, and an exploratory empirical evaluation with military professionals. Part of this framework is DIALOG, an LLM‐mediated interaction component that translates natural language into doctrine‐aligned plays, and builds up a context with ethical, legal, and operational constraints. We evaluate this framework in TNO's vehicle simulation facility, where five military professionals executed tactical missions using closed play, open play, and goal‐based delegation modes. Findings reveal a nuanced autonomy‐control trade‐off: operators initially favored higher‐autonomy modes but reverted to more structured control when confronted with unexpected or non‐doctrinal agent behaviors. The results highlight implications for MHC, transparency, and trust calibration, and point toward research directions for enhancing tactical competence, communication fidelity, and verifiability in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams.
